hints: Think about what holds the two DNA strands together and what heating to near boiling would do to those weak bonds.
After you have single strands, how would you get short starting pieces to attach at the right place when you cool the mixture down?
Recall the three temperature stages in order - very hot, then cooler, then intermediate - and match each to denaturation, annealing and extension.
Remember why Taq polymerase from a thermophilic bacterium is used instead of normal human DNA polymerase.
Link each temperature to its purpose: separating strands, providing a start site, then building new complementary strands from free nucleotides.
walkthrough:
Start with separation - denaturation**
Think of double-stranded DNA held together by hydrogen bonds between bases. Heating to 90-98 $^\circ\text{C}$ gives enough kinetic energy to break those hydrogen bonds, so the helix unwinds into two single strands. Each single strand can now act as a template.

Add starting points - annealing**
Cooling to 50-65 $^\circ\text{C}$ lets short single-stranded primers form hydrogen bonds with their complementary sequences at the ends of the target gene. Primers are essential because DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3-prime end, so they provide the binding site and starting point.

Build new copies - extension**
Warming to 65-75 $^\circ\text{C}$ gives the optimum for heat-stable Taq polymerase. It reads each template strand and joins free deoxyribonucleotides by complementary base pairing and phosphodiester bonds, synthesising two new double-stranded DNA molecules. Repeating the cycle doubles DNA each time.

Final answer: Denaturation at 90-98 $^\circ\text{C}$ breaks hydrogen bonds to separate DNA into single strands. Annealing at 50-65 $^\circ\text{C}$ allows primers to bind to complementary bases on ssDNA to provide a starting point for Taq polymerase. Extension at 65-75 $^\circ\text{C}$ when Taq polymerase joins free nucleotides to synthesise new complementary strands.

hints: The tTav gene is a mix of bacterial and viral DNA - how do genetic engineers normally cut out or build specific DNA pieces to start?
Once you have two different DNA fragments, what enzyme seals them together into one recombinant molecule, and what control sequence must be added for expression?
DNA cannot just walk into an egg on its own - think about carriers like viruses or liposomes that can deliver DNA.
Focus on the final delivery step into the mosquito egg and what must happen for the gene to be inherited by offspring.
walkthrough:
Make the recombinant gene**
You need DNA from E. coli and herpes simplex virus. This can be cut out with a restriction enzyme or made from mRNA using reverse transcriptase, or chemically synthesised from nucleotides. Then use DNA ligase to join the two sequences together by forming phosphodiester bonds, and add a promoter upstream so mosquito RNA polymerase will transcribe it later.

Package into a delivery system**
Naked DNA is broken down and poorly taken up. So load the tTav recombinant DNA into a vector - here a DNA virus is ideal because it naturally infects cells and inserts DNA, a liposome can also fuse with membranes. This protects the DNA and targets it to cells.

Transfer into eggs and integrate**
Infect the A. stephensi eggs with the virus or use microinjection directly into the egg. The vector delivers the DNA into the nucleus where it is inserted into the genome of the egg cells. That way every cell of the developing mosquito, including germ cells, carries tTav and passes it to offspring.

Final answer: Isolate bacterial and viral DNA sequences using restriction enzyme or synthesise using reverse transcriptase from mRNA. Join sequences with DNA ligase to form recombinant tTav DNA and add a promoter. Insert recombinant DNA into a vector such as virus / liposome. Infect / microinject eggs with vector so viral DNA integrates tTav gene into egg genome.

hints: To stop a gene being expressed, think about what must normally bind to DNA to start transcription.
walkthrough:
Block the start of transcription**
For a developmental gene to be expressed, a transcription factor must bind its promoter and then recruit RNA polymerase to make mRNA. If tTav protein binds to or alters the promoter or the transcription factor, RNA polymerase cannot bind and transcription is blocked, so no mRNA and no essential developmental protein is made.
Final answer: tTav protein prevents transcription factor binding to promoter / stops RNA polymerase binding to DNA, so transcription cannot occur.

hints: In the wild the gene is lethal after the larval stage, but in the lab you need live adult males to release - how could blocking tTav help?
walkthrough:
Switch off the lethal effect to rear adults**
Without tetracycline, tTav blocks essential genes and larvae die before adulthood. Tetracycline binds and inactivates tTav protein, so normal development genes are expressed. This lets lab-reared larvae survive to become adult males in large numbers, which can then be released to breed with wild females where offspring without tetracycline will die as larvae.
Final answer: Tetracycline stops action of tTav protein, so genetically modified males survive beyond larval stage and develop into adults for release.
